text: Selling pigs is a decision about net return, animal condition, feed cost, market access, and disease risk -- not just the highest quoted price. Channels include farm-gate sale to a trader/collector, a local market, or a buyer supplying a slaughterhouse/pork retailer. Keeping a pig longer for more weight doesn't automatically increase profit -- feed, labor, water, and disease risk keep accumulating, so compare the additional sale value against the additional cost of keeping the animal. CRITICAL: sick pigs, pigs from a farm with unexplained deaths, or pigs suspected of a serious contagious disease (especially ASF or CSF) must NEVER be transported to market -- movement of infected animals and contaminated equipment spreads disease. During the wet season, muddy roads complicate pig movement and hygiene; during the dry season, heat stress and dust matter most during transport. Selling a live pig is usually simpler for smallholders than processing pork themselves (no slaughter, refrigeration, or retail handling needed) -- do not assume processing into pork is automatically more profitable once labor, hygiene, and spoilage costs are included. Group marketing with nearby farmers can reduce per-animal transport cost but increases animal contact, so it should not mean unnecessarily mixing pigs from different farms, especially during suspected disease. Do not assume a specific pig breed dominates Preah Vihear -- record the farmer's or supplier's actual information. Never invent a current pig price, guaranteed profitable selling weight, disease diagnosis, or ASF/CSF status for a particular village.
